title: Organic Search Is Shrinking, While Email Builds a More Durable Audience
author: Ali Farhat
summary: Organic discovery is becoming a less dependable single source of website visits in the data examined by Search Engine Land. At the same time, email is growing in both absolute visits and year-over-year performance, giving publishers, brands, and ecommerce sites a stronger reason to invest in audiences they can reach without relying entirely on a search results page. In Kevin Indig's Search Engine Land analysis of Similarweb data , email visits rose from January through August 2026 compared with the same period in 2025. The analysis also found that direct and organic traffic declined over a longer two-year comparison. The evidence does not mean search has stopped mattering. It does suggest that visibility in search and AI-generated answers should increasingly support a broader audience-development model rather than stand alone. What the Similarweb analysis found The analysis covered roughly 1,896 to 1,897 domains, depending on the comparison. It is therefore an observed sample, not a measure of every site or all web traffic. For January through August 2026 versus the same months in 2025, email visits increased 16.3% in the United States and 17.0% in France. Paid search also grew in the reported data, by 20.8% in the U.S. and 20.3% in France, although those figures require important attribution context. Email was already larger than paid search in total visits in both markets examined: Market Email visits Paid-search visits United States 3.94 billion 3.70 billion France 462 million 401 million Direct remained the largest channel in the analysis, but it was shrinking. Direct visits were down 2.7% year over year in the U.S. and 3.1% in France for January through August. From August 2024 to August 2026, direct visits declined 3.4% in the U.S. and 5.3% in France. Organic visits fell more sharply over that latter period: 13.2% in the U.S. and 23.4% in France. These are not proof that every website is losing organic traffic or that email will outperform every other channel. They are a useful directional signal from the domains studied, particularly for teams whose acquisition plans still assume organic traffic will be the primary scalable source of returning attention. Why paid-search measurement needs caution One of the most valuable parts of the analysis is its warning about routing and attribution. Paid-search estimates can change depending on how visits through Google's googleadservices.com ad-tracking domain are categorized. When that domain was included, reported paid-search growth was 13.5% in the U.S. and 10.7% in France. When it was excluded, paid-search growth rose to 21.0% in the U.S. and 15.2% in France. In those comparisons, email growth was reported at 20.5% in the U.S. and 17.6% in France. The discrepancy is a reminder that channel labels are not always clean descriptions of user behavior. Redirects, tracking domains, analytics configuration, consent choices, apps, and users moving between channels can all influence what is credited to organic, paid, direct, referral, or email. For marketers, the practical lesson is not to disregard channel reports. It is to avoid treating a single channel line item as a complete causal explanation. Compare analytics platforms and tagging rules, document changes in tracking, and evaluate acquisition alongside downstream engagement and repeat visits. Search visibility should feed an owned-audience strategy Organic search, Google AI Overviews, AI Mode, ChatGPT Search, and other answer engines can still introduce people to a brand. But discovery is different from a durable audience relationship. A citation, ranking, or mention may generate awareness without creating a reliable path back to the site. That makes first-party audience capture more strategically important. A useful visitor journey has two connected stages: Earn discovery by publishing accessible, credible content that search engines and AI systems can understand and cite. Give the visitor a meaningful reason to return through an email subscription, account, saved resource, product update, or another permission-based relationship. Email is particularly notable in the Similarweb analysis because it is both an owned communication channel and a source of measurable repeat visits. It does not remove dependence on platforms entirely. Delivery, inbox placement, and subscriber consent still matter. However, it gives a business a route to its audience that is not contingent on appearing in the next search result or AI answer. Direct traffic deserves similar attention, even though it declined in the reported data. Direct is a mixed category, not a pure measure of brand loyalty. It can include untagged campaigns and other traffic that analytics cannot classify. Still, rising repeat visits, bookmarked access, and branded return behavior are generally useful indicators that a site is building recognition beyond one-time search clicks. Practical steps for websites adapting to weaker organic growth The appropriate response is diversification, not abandoning SEO or treating email as a replacement for search. Search content can create the demand that makes subscriptions and repeat visits possible. The goal is to make the channels reinforce each other. Start by reviewing which high-value organic landing pages attract new visitors but fail to create a next step. Add relevant, low-friction subscription opportunities that match the page's topic or user need. A newsletter about the subject, a product-update list, or a recurring research digest can be more useful than a generic sign-up request. Next, separate discovery metrics from relationship metrics. Track organic entrances, AI referral traffic where it is identifiable, email-driven sessions, returning users, branded search interest, and conversions. Do not assume a fall in last-click organic traffic means search content has no role in subsequent email sign-ups or direct returns. Finally, audit attribution before changing budgets. The googleadservices.com finding illustrates how much channel interpretation can depend on classification. Maintain consistent UTM conventions, review redirect behavior, and annotate major tracking or consent changes when comparing periods. If AI search reduces clicks for some informational queries, this approach becomes even more relevant. The content that earns visibility should also demonstrate enough expertise and usefulness that the people who do click choose to establish a direct relationship. GEO Search Leads can help teams turn AI-search visibility into a more deliberate website strategy by assessing GEO readiness and surfacing optimization opportunities in content that supports discovery. If you want a clearer starting point for improving how your site is understood across generative search experiences, create a GEO Search Leads account . Frequently Asked Questions Does this analysis show that organic search is declining for every website? No. The analysis reports trends across a sample of roughly 1,896 to 1,897 domains in the U.S. and France. Performance can differ significantly by site, market, content type, and measurement setup. Why did paid-search growth change when googleadservices.com was included or excluded? Google's ad-tracking domain can affect how visits are routed and categorized in traffic data. The analysis found materially different paid-search growth rates under the two treatments, showing that attribution rules affect interpretation. Is direct traffic a reliable measure of brand loyalty? Not by itself. Direct traffic can include bookmarked visits and people intentionally returning to a brand, but it can also include traffic that analytics could not attribute to another source. It is best evaluated alongside branded search, email engagement, and returning-user behavior. Should businesses replace SEO with email marketing? No. The data supports diversifying acquisition and building owned audience relationships, not replacing search. SEO and GEO can support discovery, while email provides a way to maintain contact with interested visitors. Conclusion The Similarweb findings point to a practical shift in priorities: organic visibility remains valuable, but it is less safe as the sole foundation for audience growth. Sites that connect search and AI discovery to permission-based email relationships, repeat visits, and disciplined attribution will be better positioned to understand and reduce their dependence on any one traffic source.

title: Metadata CSVs, Upload Ledgers, and Covers: The Four Scripts Behind 39 Products
author: Muhamad Revanza Rafif Hamdani
summary: Last October I ran my batch upload twice. Same folder, same command, eleven hours apart. I had forgotten which assets I had already submitted to Adobe Stock, so I re-ran the whole thing. Adobe's review caught the duplicates and my account got a warning. That warning is the reason upload_tracker.py exists. This post is about the four scripts that keep my pipeline from making that kind of mistake again, and what I learned packaging 39 products with them. The CSV header is a contract, not a suggestion Every stock platform validates your metadata file before it even looks at your images. Adobe Stock wants a five-column CSV with an exact header order. Vecteezy wants four columns. Dreamstime wants fifteen. Get one column wrong, or put the header in the wrong order, and the upload is rejected before your art is ever reviewed. No partial credit. My first month, I wrote these CSVs by hand in a spreadsheet. I got the Adobe header right eventually, then pasted it into the Vecteezy file and got rejected, because the column count was wrong. That was the moment I stopped hand-editing and wrote make_metadata.py . You point it at a folder of files, tell it the platform, and it writes the header that platform demands, and nothing else: python make_metadata.py ./my-assets --platform adobe --out metadata.csv --ext .jpg python make_metadata.py ./my-assets --platform vecteezy --out vecteezy.csv --ext .jpg python make_metadata.py ./my-assets --platform dreamstime --out dreamstime.csv --ext .jpg By default it title-cases the filename and uses that as the title. That is fine for a first pass, but replace it before you submit. I keep a titles.json with real titles and keywords per asset, and pass it with --titles . The script uses only the Python standard library. No install, no dependencies, nothing to break. The ledger that stops double-posting The double-post incident taught me that memory is not a system. Now every asset that goes to a channel gets logged in a plain text ledger by upload_tracker.py : python upload_tracker.py pending items.txt # what is NOT done yet python upload_tracker.py done "asset-001.jpg" python upload_tracker.py status Before any batch run, I check pending first. The re-run problem is gone because the re-run reads the same ledger. This is the least glamorous script in the kit and the one that has saved me the most trouble. It also uses the standard library alone. Turning a document into a product Half my products are not art at all, they are documents. Checklists, guides, templates with instructions. The content existed as Markdown long before it looked sellable. The gap between "I have a good doc" and "I have a product" is formatting, and md2pdf.py closes it in one command: python md2pdf.py content.md product.pdf "My Product Title" It handles headings, tables, lists, and links, using reportlab under the hood. That is one of only two third-party packages in the whole kit. The other is Pillow. Everything else is standard library, which matters more than it sounds, because dependency rot kills small pipelines quietly. Packaging: a zip with a real cover A bare file does not sell. A zip with a proper cover does. pack_product.py bundles the product folder and renders two images: a 1280x720 cover and a 600x600 thumbnail: python pack_product.py my-product "My Product" "A short subtitle" 9 It writes my-product.zip , the cover, and the thumbnail into a _system folder, and you can redirect that with --dir or the PACK_ROOT environment variable. Pillow renders the images. Two sizes, fixed dimensions, done. I stopped agonizing over covers once I accepted that a clean, consistent template beats a unique design every time. The tiny server rules None of this ran on a beefy machine. The whole pipeline runs on 1 vCPU, 2 GB RAM, no GPU. That constraint forced habits that are worth more than the hardware they replaced: One process at a time. Never fan out image jobs in parallel on a single core. It does not go faster, it just thrashes. Call gc.collect() after each asset. Python will not free memory promptly on its own, and on a 2 GB box that adds up over a batch of a few hundred files. Measure peak RSS, not average. resource.getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss tells you the real ceiling. Average memory numbers lied to me twice before I started watching the peak. One file per subprocess for heavy render steps, so memory is actually returned to the OS between items. Render at the resolution you need. Inspecting a preview at 60 dpi instead of 300 cut one render step's memory use dramatically. The full catalogue so far is 39 products, about 856 MB of output, built on top of roughly 19,000 lines of pipeline code and over 300 pages of research behind the rules these scripts enforce. The folder layout that keeps it sane The last thing that matters is structure. A catalogue becomes a junk drawer without fixed folders, so the kit assumes one: project/ assets/ raw output, one file per asset output/ ready-to-submit files + metadata.csv packs/ finished zips + covers research/ notes and sources scripts/ these tools One warning from a mistake I made exactly once: keep research/ forever. Your notes and logs are the raw material for future products. I deleted a research folder during a cleanup pass and spent a weekend reconstructing it. That will not happen again. These four scripts are the packaging layer of a larger system. Under them sits a free stack: Hermes Agent as the orchestrator that schedules jobs and retries failures, and 9Router as a local proxy for LLM access, both at zero cost. But the packaging layer is where most solo makers stall, and it is the part I use every single week. I wrote all of this up, with the scripts themselves, as the ai sticker factory playbook. It is the tool built from this work, not a tutorial that ends at "here's how you'd do it". If any of the failure modes above sound familiar, it will save you the warnings I earned the hard way. title: Testing Your Metadata CSV Against Adobe, Vecteezy And Dreamstime Before Upload
author: Muhamad Revanza Rafif Hamdani
summary: I lost an entire Saturday to a CSV header. Not to the art. Not to keywords. To one row of column names. I had 40 files ready for Adobe Stock, a metadata file I'd built by hand in a spreadsheet, and the uploader rejected it in about two seconds. The reason: Adobe's CSV wants exactly five columns, in a fixed order, and I had six. One extra column, "notes", that I thought would be harmless. It wasn't. The parser reads the header, sees a shape it doesn't expect, and stops before it ever looks at your actual files. That was the moment I stopped hand-building metadata files and wrote a script to do it instead. Here's what I learned testing that script against all three platforms. Each platform wants a different shape, and the shape is not documented well Adobe is the strictest and the simplest. Five columns: filename, title, keywords, category, releases. Get the count wrong or the order wrong and the upload fails before review. There's no partial credit. My script, make_metadata.py , writes those five columns and nothing else. No extra columns "for my own reference". If I want notes, they live in a separate file, not in the CSV I feed the uploader. Vecteezy takes four columns. Dreamstime takes fifteen. Fifteen. That one includes fields Adobe doesn't ask for at all, and if you've only ever built the Adobe file, the Dreamstime one will trip you up because you can't just reorder what you have. The script builds each one from the same folder of assets, so the source of truth is the files themselves plus a titles JSON, and the three CSVs are just projections of it. The command looks like this, once per platform: python make_metadata.py ./my-assets --platform adobe --out metadata.csv --ext .jpg python make_metadata.py ./my-assets --platform vecteezy --out vecteezy.csv --ext .jpg python make_metadata.py ./my-assets --platform dreamstime --out dreamstime.csv --ext .jpg Without a titles file it title-cases the filename as a placeholder. That's fine for a dry run, but I replace it before submitting. A filename is not a title, and reviewers can tell. Test with one file, not forty My second failure was batching. I generated metadata for 40 files, uploaded all of them, and found out afterward that half my titles were too long and several keyword lists had formatting problems. Now I always do this: build the CSV for a single test file, run it through the platform's uploader or validator, confirm it passes, then run the full batch. It costs ten minutes and has saved me from three bad batches so far. The other thing I test for is the header itself. I keep the exact header row each platform expects in the script, so the output always starts with the right columns. If Adobe changes their format, I fix one line in one place instead of rebuilding a spreadsheet. The double-post problem is worse than the rejection problem A rejected CSV wastes an evening. A double-posted asset can flag your account. This happened to a friend of mine, not to me, which is why I built the guard before I needed it: upload_tracker.py is a plain ledger of what has been posted. Before any batch, I run: python upload_tracker.py pending items.txt and it shows me what is genuinely new. After posting, I mark each item done. If a script re-runs by accident, or I forget which batch went out on Tuesday, the ledger remembers, not me. It uses only the Python standard library, so there's nothing to install and nothing to break. Where the actual bottleneck sits None of this is compute. My whole pipeline, the one that produced 39 finished products and 856 MB of output, ran on 1 vCPU and 2 GB RAM with no GPU. The hard parts are boring: the exact header each platform demands, the discipline of one test file before a batch, and a ledger so a re-run can't hurt you. The metadata script and the tracker together use zero third-party packages. The only installs in the whole kit are Pillow for cover rendering and reportlab for PDF output, and neither touches the metadata path. One habit worth stealing: keep the raw research. I have 300+ pages of notes behind the rules these scripts enforce, and I once deleted a research folder to "clean up" and regretted it within a month. Notes are the raw material for the next product. Disk space is cheap. Rebuilding a scrape log is not. What I actually built After the third platform rejected a file for a reason I'd already fixed on another platform, I stopped patching spreadsheets and wrote the scripts properly. They're now the packaging layer of my pipeline: make_metadata.py for the Adobe 5-column, Vecteezy 4-column and Dreamstime 15-column CSVs, upload_tracker.py for the ledger, plus md2pdf.py and pack_product.py for turning documents and asset folders into sellable products with covers and thumbnails. I've collected them, with the folder layout and the small-server RAM notes, into the pipeline starter kit. It's the tool built from this work, nothing more.
